title: Brazil pauses at 13.75% as inflation expectations rise despite sharper cyclical slowing
summary: Brazil’s Copom held the Selic at 13.75% on 4 November. Seven participants supported the decision. The statement presented a substantially restrictive rate, stronger signs of domestic slowing and a deterioration in price stability at the same time. Headline inflation and the average underlying measures had accelerated above the upper limit of the tolerance interval. Focus inflation expectations had moved further from target, reaching 5.2% for 2026 and 4.8% for 2027. The committee saw a case for preserving the existing degree of restraint even as the cost of doing so became more visible in interest-sensitive sectors.

The domestic split was important. Activity had weakened more markedly, especially in cyclical sectors. The labour market remained resilient but had begun to soften at the margin. The committee still judged the indicators consistent with slower activity over 2026. It also continued to see a positive output gap as a potential source of services inflation. These statements refer to different objects. A slowing growth rate does not establish the level of spare capacity, and initial cooling in employment can take time to reach wages and service prices. The committee did not identify a particular unemployment or GDP threshold that would allow easing to resume.

The international backdrop was more adverse. The prolonged Middle Eastern conflict had pushed up oil and refined-product prices, and advanced-economy monetary policy had become more restrictive. Commodity and asset-price volatility mattered both directly to domestic prices and indirectly through the currency and global financial conditions. Longer-term inflation expectations could incorporate second-round effects from energy or climate-related agricultural and electricity costs. Consumption stimulus, persistent services inflation and an exchange rate weaker than the reference path could add pressure. On the other side of the risk distribution, a deeper domestic or global slowdown and lower commodity prices could accelerate disinflation. The committee continued to judge the balance asymmetric to the upside.

The reference scenario quantified the change in outlook. Four-quarter headline IPCA was projected at 5.6% in 2026, 4.7% in 2027 and 3.5% in the second quarter of 2028, the new relevant endpoint. Market-determined prices were projected at 5.5%, 4.8% and 3.4%. Administered prices started higher at 6.0%, fell to 4.2% in 2027 and remained at 3.9% at the endpoint. Administered prices contributed to near-term pressure, while market-determined prices carried more inflation through calendar 2027. The committee’s 5.6% projection was 0.4 percentage point above the current-year survey, whereas its 2027 forecast was 0.1 point below the corresponding Focus expectation. Comparing its Q2 2028 projection with a survey for calendar 2027 would mix a disagreement over inflation with different end dates.

Copom explicitly reminded readers that its projection used the Focus path for the Selic and incorporated supply shocks since the last meeting. It started the exchange rate at BRL 5.20 per dollar, applied purchasing power parity thereafter and assumed oil followed futures for six months before rising 2% per year. The December electricity tariff flag was green for 2026 and 2027. Those assumptions matter for interpreting the 6.0% administered-price projection: the green flag concerns one element and cannot by itself establish why the full category rose. Similarly, the table is conditional on a surveyed rate path and cannot be read as a forecast under unchanged rates indefinitely.

The hold gave investors a policy outcome but no duration for the pause. It would be meaningful to ask whether markets revised the expected next move, the period of restrictive rates, or the premium they demanded for long-term inflation risk. Domestic weakening, tighter foreign policy and the oil shock all act on the same assets. The statement contains no announcement-window prices with which to assign the move to any one factor.

questions.question: Can further cyclical weakness relieve services inflation before expectations become more entrenched?
questions.detail: Pair sector output and credit-sensitive spending with hours, wage agreements and service-price changes. Track expectations at fixed calendar horizons, together with dispersion in forecasts. The timing matters: a lagged decline in wage and services pressure would support the case for waiting, while persistent repricing despite softer hiring would imply costlier disinflation.

questions.question: Which prices carry most of the projected persistence into 2027 and 2028?
questions.detail: Reconstruct administered-price schedules and compare them with market services, food and freight exposure under alternative oil, currency and electricity assumptions. Keep calendar years distinct from the four quarters ending in mid-2028. The published baseline shows that different components dominate at different points but gives no numerical decomposition of the new shocks.

questions.question: Did the pause extend the expected period of restraint or primarily alter inflation risk compensation?
questions.detail: Compare pricing for the next two meetings with later nominal forwards and inflation-linked prices in a narrow release window. Document simultaneous news on global monetary policy, oil and the exchange rate. A rise in longer nominal yields can reflect either a higher expected short-rate path or additional compensation for uncertain inflation. The most informative cross-check is whether surveyed expectations of the future policy rate moved in the same direction as the forward curve.
